                                                Abstract
     We study the extent to which wide neural networks may be approximated by Gaussian
     processes, when initialized with random weights. It is a well-established fact that as the
     width of a network goes to infinity, its law converges to that of a Gaussian process. We
     make this quantitative by establishing explicit convergence rates for the central limit the-
     orem in an infinite-dimensional functional space, metrized with a natural transportation
     distance. We identify two regimes of interest; when the activation function is polynomial,
     its degree determines the rate of convergence, while for non-polynomial activations, the
     rate is governed by the smoothness of the function.


1. Introduction
In the past decade, artificial neural networks have experienced an unprecedented renais-
sance. However, the current theory has yet to catch-up with the practice and cannot explain
their impressive performance. Particularly intriguing is the fact that over-parameterized
models do not tend to over-fit, even when trained to zero error on the training set. Owing
to this seemingly paradoxical fact, researchers have focused on understanding the infinite-
width limit of neural networks. This line of research has led to many important discoveries
such as the ‘lazy-training’ regime Chizat et al. (2019); Tzen and Raginsky (2020) which
is governed by the limiting ‘neural tangent kernel’ (see Jacot et al. (2018)), as well as the
‘mean-field’ limit approach (see Mei et al. (2018, 2019); Karakida et al. (2019) for some
examples) to study the training dynamics and loss landscape.
    The first to study the limiting distribution of a neural network at (a random) initial-
ization was Neal (Neal, 1996), who proved a Central Limit Theorem (CLT) for two-layered
wide neural networks. According to Neal’s result, when initialized with random weights, as
the width of the network goes to infinity, its law converges, in distribution, to a Gaussian
process. Subsequent works have generalized this result to deeper networks and other ar-
chitectures (Williams (1997); Matthews et al. (2018); Novak et al. (2018); Garriga-Alonso
et al. (2018); Hazan and Jaakkola (2015); Yang (2019a,b)). We also mention the work
of Matsubara et al. (2020), which considered the problem of finding an appropriate ran-
dom initialization that gives rise to valid approximations for Gaussian processes with a
pre-determined covariance structure. This correspondence between Gaussian processes and

neural networks has proved to be highly influential and has inspired many new models (see
Yang (2019a) for a thorough review of these models).
    Towards supplying a theoretical framework to study real world neural networks, one
important challenge is to understand the extent to which existing asymptotic results, which
essentially only apply to infinite networks, may also be applied to finite ones. While there
have been several works in this direction (c.f. Arora et al. (2019); Geiger et al. (2020);
Hanin (2019); Andreassen and Dyer (2020); Yaida (2019); Antognini (2019); Aitken and
Gur-Ari (2020); Bracale et al. (2021)), to the best of our knowledge, all known results
consider finite-dimensional marginals of the random process and the question of finding a
finite-width quantitative analog to Neal’s CLT, which applies in a functional space, has
remained open. The main goal of this paper is to tackle this question.
    In essence, we prove a quantitative CLT in the space of functions. On a first glance, this
is a completely different setting than the classical CLT, even in high-dimensional regimes.
The function space is infinite-dimensional, while all quantitative bounds of CLT deterio-
rate with the dimension (Bobkov (2018); Courtade et al. (2019); Bonis (2020)). However,
by exploiting the special structure of neural networks we are able to reduce the problem
to finite-dimensional sets, where we capitalize on recent advances made in understanding
the rate of convergence of the high-dimensional CLT. In particular, we give quantitative
bounds, depending on the network’s width and the dimension of the input, which show
that, when initialized randomly, wide but finite networks can be well-approximated by a
Gaussian process. The functional nature of our results essentially means that when consid-
ering the joint distribution attained on a finite set of inputs to the function, ours bounds
do not deteriorate as the number of input points increases.

Roughly speaking, we prove the following results:

   • We first consider two-layered networks with polynomial activation functions. By em-
     bedding the network into a high-dimensional tensor space we prove a quantitative
     CLT, with a polynomial rate of convergence in a strong transportation metric.

   • We next consider general activations and show that under a (very mild) integrability
     assumption, one can reduce this case to the polynomial case. This is done at the cost
     of weakening the transportation distance. The rate of convergence depends on the
     smoothness of the activation and is typically sub-polynomial.

     Let us remark about the methods of proof and the technical contributions. Whereas
existing proofs of Gaussian behavior of neural networks apply the central limit theorem on
finite dimensional marginals, our proof needs to be different, since we have to apply the CLT
to a representation of the function itself (which does not depend on input points). We do
this by embedding the network in a finite dimensional Wiener chaos, and invoking a CLT for
high dimensions in those spaces. As far as we are aware, this is the first work to follow such
a strategy. In order to apply off-the-shelf central limit theorems to our framework, we need
to prove results concerning the covariance structures and variance bounds for polynomials.
It is plausible that the idea of using Wiener chaos, as well as our implementation of it, could
be useful outside the scope of this work.
